## What Are Those Terms?

### 🔍 Domain Name Registration Basics 🎯
Domain names are addresses humans recognize (example.org, google.co.uk, www.example.com)—they look very familiar even to strangers visiting your webpage. They essentially map back home via HTTP protocols (`http`, `ftp`).

#### How It Works
When you create a domain, you assign it to a registrar (reseller platform): registrars manage WHOIS records linking registered DNS entries together. Every subsequent entry needs updating periodically ("DNS updates") until the domain resolves successfully. Free/free-domains resellers handle part of this, saving money compared to buying new ones from TLD registries.

This isn't always easy for beginners. There are common mistakes: registering accidentally creates duplicate subdomains (*sub*.com), choosing obscure-looking names risks brand dilution, and forgetting to renew pays-per-year subscriptions regularly causes downtime—or worse, expired periods where sites stay offline.

Some opt-in solutions include creating private aliases locally (if you trust local networks) or setting automatic renewal triggers via email notifications.

---

### 💼 Hosting Services Overview ⚙️
Hosting involves providing Internet Protocol communication channels for clients accessing your website. Providers sell hosted environments ranging from shared cloud setups for smaller projects to premium VPS/Virtual Private Server configurations tailored to bigger operations requiring continuous uptime tracking.

Shared hosts (often referred to casually) deliver public IP space and limited resources initially—it saves you upfront hosting costs while giving control over settings and security configuration afterward. Premium plans tend to include monitoring, analytics dashboards, backup restoration features, SSL certificates, and advanced threat detection—all essential for growing commerce-heavy e-commerce storefronts.

However, shared-hosting can leave little room for customization if you ever shift budget priorities or expand functionality. Most experienced owners choose between shared clouds for simplicity and paid SaaS vendors (such as Netlify, Vercel, GoDaddy Pro) when demand grows consistently.

These differences mean planning seriously beforehand rather than jumping blindly toward whichever option suits your immediate capacity level.

Since you're running a bakery, expect visitors coming mainly from physical locations (local farmers markets, cafes nearby) and possibly food delivery apps or social media reviews counting towards sales revenue—a dynamic customer base that shifts year-round.

Knowing your core buyer behavior lets you match the appropriate tier sooner rather than waiting for market saturation signals.

Bakery logistics span inventory ordering (from bulk suppliers to stockroom staff handling orders), order fulfillment systems (some require custom integration late), payment gateways (credit cards, giftcards, digital wallets differ greatly), shipping methods (FedEx/delivery/voucher programs fall squarely outside direct lines!), and internal accounting controls (general ledger accounts—even handwritten—are needed eventually).
